claim: 41 cell types during B- and T-cell development have an experimentally established developmental lineage.
source: We analyzed gene expression data from 41 cell types during B- and T- cell development that have an experimentally established developmental lineage (Figure 1A, Heng et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Heng et al., 2008 and reference to Figure 1A showing the lineage tree.

claim: 150 triplets of cell types with experimentally verified lineage relationships were identified from B- and T-cell development.
source: We identified 150 triplets of cell types with experimentally verified lineage relationships from B- and T- cell development (Heng et al., 2008) (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Heng et al., 2008 and reference to source data.

claim: 56% of triplets contained more than 10 genes exhibiting the clear minimum pattern.
source: 56% of the triplets contained more than 10 genes exhibiting the clear minimum pattern, and in 100% of these triplets the majority of genes with expression fitting this pattern reached their minimum expression in one of the leaves (Figure 1C) and never in the root of the triplet.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In 100% of triplets with more than 10 genes exhibiting the clear minimum pattern, the majority of genes reached their minimum expression in one of the leaves and never in the root.
source: 56% of the triplets contained more than 10 genes exhibiting the clear minimum pattern, and in 100% of these triplets the majority of genes with expression fitting this pattern reached their minimum expression in one of the leaves (Figure 1C) and never in the root of the triplet.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The clear maximum pattern was a poorer indicator of lineage relationships than the clear minimum pattern.
source: The clear maximum pattern was a poorer indicator of lineage relationships (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 83% of triplets had more than 10 genes exhibiting the clear maximum pattern.
source: 83% of the triplets had more than 10 genes exhibiting this pattern, but 10% of those showed the majority of genes with expression fitting this pattern reaching their maximum in the root while the others did so in the leaves.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis of the clear maximum pattern.

claim: The integrity of the relationship between the clear maximum pattern and lineage topology was not correlated with the number of genes exhibiting the pattern.
source: Crucially, the integrity of the relationship between the clear maximum pattern and lineage topology was not correlated with the number of genes exhibiting the pattern (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Genes exhibiting the clear minimum pattern include many known to be functionally important for lineage decisions.
source: There are many examples of genes known to be functionally important for lineage decisions whose expression patterns fit the clear minimum pattern.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of developmental biology and examples provided in the text.

claim: In lateral inhibition, progenitor cells express genes together (e.g., Notch and Delta) which are differentially expressed in differentiated states.
source: In the case of lateral inhibition commonly used during development, progenitor cells express genes together (for example, Notch and Delta) which are differentially expressed in the differentiated states (only Notch or only Delta) (Perrimon et al., 2012) reaching the minimum expression level in one of the leaves.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Perrimon et al., 2012.

claim: The clear minimum pattern is consistent with mutual inhibition mechanisms in development.
source: The same pattern is also seen in multiple examples of lineage decisions often involving mutual inhibition, where key genes expressed in the progenitor are differentially regulated in the progeny (Graf and Enver, 2009; Qi et al., 2013; Thomson et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: PCA analysis failed to reconstruct lineage relationships between all cell types in B- and T-cell development.
source: Indeed, our attempt to reconstruct the lineage relationships between all cell types using methods based on PCA failed (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the PCA analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Unrelated triplets show genes exhibiting a clear minimum evenly distributed amongst the cell types.
source: We found that while there were a substantial number of genes exhibiting a clear minimum in one of the three cell types in unrelated triplets, their minima were evenly distributed amongst the cell types.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of 100 unrelated triplets.

claim: Unrelated triplets have higher entropy than related triplets in the distribution of genes showing the clear minimum pattern.
source: The unrelated triplets have higher entropy and typically more genes with a minimum level.
evidence: The claim is supported by entropy analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The probability of obtaining the null topology differs between related and unrelated triplets with an AUC of 0.96.
source: The distribution of the probability of obtaining the null topology was considerably different between the related triplets and the unrelated triplets, with an AUC of 0.96 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC curve analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B–C.

claim: The triplet CMP/ST/MPP has an 84% probability that ST is the intermediate cell type.
source: Using Equation 1 above and assuming a sparsity parameter of 0.05, we calculate that there is an 84% chance that the topology is ST (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Bayesian inference calculation shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Transition genes for triplet CMP-ST-MPP include Gata1, Dach1, Gata2, Hlf, Tsc22d1, and Hoxa9.
source: Figure 2D shows the names and associated probabilities of the 12 genes most likely to be transition genes for the triplet CMP−ST−MPP. The transition genes fall into two groups, corresponding to the two groups in Figure 2B. One group, which includes genes Gata1, Dach1, and Gata2, has higher expression in CMP than in MPP; the other group, which includes Hlf, Tsc22d1, and Hoxa9, has higher expression in MPP.
evidence: The claim is supported by probabilistic analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Many transition genes identified include genes previously identified as important for lineage specification.
source: Although the values of the probabilities of the genes being transition genes vary with the value of the sparsity parameter, the relative order of different genes does not change. The genes identified include many genes previously identified as being important for lineage specification (Crispino, 2005; Gazit et al., 2013; Miyawaki et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on lineage specification.

claim: Marker genes for ST include Mpl and Rai14.
source: In addition to the transition genes, we identified marker genes (p(αi=1 | {gi},T)>0.8) present only in ST (including Mpl and Rai14, consistent with [Solar et al., 1998]) and then symmetrically downregulated in both CMP and MPP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by probabilistic analysis and citation to Solar et al., 1998.

claim: Marker genes for CMP include Srf, Zeb2, Rbpj and Irf8.
source: Marker genes for CMP include Srf, Zeb2, Rbpj and Irf8 (consistent with [Goossens et al., 2011; Kurotaki et al., 2013; Ragu et al., 2010; Robert-Moreno et al., 2005; Tamura et al., 2000])
evidence: The claim is supported by probabilistic analysis and citations to published work.

claim: Marker genes for MPP include Satb1.
source: marker genes for MPP include Satb1, consistent with (Satoh et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by probabilistic analysis and citation to Satoh et al., 2013.

claim: For triplet MEP/GMP/FrBC, the most likely topology is the null hypothesis with 99% probability.
source: In contrast to the case of the triplet of cell types CMP/ST/MPP, for triplet MEP/GMP/FrBC, the distributions of genes supporting different topologies are similar (Figure 2F). Thus the most likely topology calculated using Equation 1 is the null hypothesis (99%), which is that transition genes, if they exist, do not have patterns that depend on the cellular topology (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by Bayesian inference calculation shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Out of 165 possible triplets of hematopoietic progenitors, 144 showed one single non-null topology with probability greater than 0.6.
source: Out of the 165 possible triplets of hematopoietic progenitors, 144 showed one single non-null topology with probability greater than 0.6 over a range of the prior odds from 10−6 to 102.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of all possible triplets.

claim: The inferred lineage tree supports the Adolfsson model of early hematopoiesis.
source: The lineage tree that we determined is consistent with the Adolfsson model and contains three additional lineage decisions (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the inferred lineage tree shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The topology of triplet ST/MPP/CMP distinguishes between the traditional model and the Adolfsson model of hematopoiesis.
source: The ST/CMP/MPP triplet (Figure 2B–E) immediately distinguishes between two competing models regarding the hierarchy of early hematopoietic progenitors.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the triplet topology analysis.

claim: The inferred topology CMP-ST-MPP supports the Adolfsson model where ST splits into CMP and MPP.
source: We identify both CMP – ST – MPP and CMP – LT – MPP as the correct topologies, lending support to the Adolfsson model.
evidence: The claim is supported by the inferred triplet topologies.

claim: The inferred expected topologies of 8 out of 9 triplets that differ between the Adolfsson and traditional models support the Adolfsson model.
source: The Adolfsson and traditional models differ in the topology of 9 triplets. The inferred expected topologies of 8 out of these nine triplets support the Adolfsson model, which led to the identification of the final tree (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of triplet topologies shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: CMP gives rise to MEP and GMP in the inferred hematopoietic lineage tree.
source: The lineage tree that we determined is consistent with the Adolfsson model and contains three additional lineage decisions (Figure 3A–B). First, CMP gives rise to MEP (megakaryocyte/erythroid progenitor) and GMP (granulocyte/macrophage progenitor).
evidence: The claim is supported by the inferred lineage tree shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: MPP gives rise to MLP, which then splits into GMP and CLP in the inferred hematopoietic lineage tree.
source: Second, MPP gives rise to MLP (multilineage progenitor), which then splits into the GMP and CLP (common lymphoid progenitor) cell types.
evidence: The claim is supported by the inferred lineage tree.

claim: CLP gives rise to ETP and FrA in the inferred hematopoietic lineage tree.
source: In the final lineage decision, CLP gives rise to the ETP (pre-T) and FrA (pre-pro-B) cell types.
evidence: The claim is supported by the inferred lineage tree.

claim: Among 14 triplets containing only adjacent cell types, an average of 24 marker genes per cell type and 25 transition genes were identified.
source: Among the 14 triplets that contained only adjacent cell types, we identified on average 24 marker genes per cell type and 25 transition genes (probability threshold of 0.8, prior odds p(βi=1)/p(βi=0) =0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of triplets in the hematopoietic lineage tree.

claim: Many identified transition and marker genes are known to be functionally important, including Cebpa, Sfpi1, Gata1, Satb1, Irf8 and Ebf1.
source: Many genes we discovered as belonging with high probability to the transition and marker classes of genes at each lineage decision are known in the literature to be functionally important genes, including classic hematopoietic regulators such as Cebpa, Sfpi1, Gata1, Satb1, Irf8 and Ebf1 (see full tables with references in Figure 3C and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by literature references provided in Figure 3C.

claim: Identified genes include many successfully used in hematopoietic reprogramming experiments, including Gata2 and Pbx1.
source: Additionally, the genes identified include many genes successfully used in hematopoietic reprogramming experiments, including Gata2 and Pbx1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to reprogramming experiments in Figure 3C.

claim: The inferred intestinal lineage tree differs from Grün et al. only in the progression from crypt base columnar cells to Goblet cell populations.
source: The only disagreement between the two methods is the progression from crypt base columnar cells (C2) to different populations of Goblet cells (C4 and C8). Grun et al. hypothesize a C2 – C8 – C4 progression, while we infer the triplet C8 – C2 – C4 with p>0.99, suggesting that the progenitor C2 gives rise to both differentiated Goblet subpopulations.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with Grün et al.'s method.

claim: High probability transition genes in intestinal development include Klf4, Atoh1, Spdef, Foxa1/Foxa2, and Tcf3.
source: The high probability transition genes included many factors well known for their roles in tissue homeostasis and development (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), notably Klf4 (Yu et al., 2012), Atoh1 (VanDussen and Samuelson, 2010), Spdef (Noah et al., 2010), Foxa1/Foxa2 (Ye and Kaestner, 2009), and Tcf3 (Merrill et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and citations to published work.

claim: Single-cell gene expression data from 2217 cells from in vitro human neuronal development were analyzed.
source: To study the latter, we analyzed single-cell gene expression data from 2217 cells from an in vitro differentiation protocol for early human neuronal development (Yao et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Yao et al., 2017.

claim: Human embryonic stem cells were subjected to SMAD inhibition-based cortical induction, progenitor expansion, and neural differentiation phases.
source: Briefly, human embryonic stem cells (hESCs) were subjected to a SMAD inhibition-based cortical induction phase, a progenitor expansion phase, and a neural differentiation phase.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol used.

claim: Single cells were sorted at 12, 26, 54, and 80 days into differentiation and profiled using SMART-Seq2.
source: Single cells were sorted at 12, 26, 54, and 80 days into differentiation, and their gene expression was profiled using the SMART-Seq2 technique (Picelli et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental protocol and cites the SMART-Seq2 technique.

claim: t-SNE clustering showed separation by day and SOX2 expression but the number of predicted clusters varied depending on the perplexity parameter.
source: In the initial clustering of the single-cell data, dimensionality reduction by PCA (into 15 above-noise components) followed by t-SNE (Van Der Maaten and Hinton, 2008; Satija et al., 2015) showed separation by day and SOX2 expression (Figure 4A). However, the number of predicted clusters varied depending on the perplexity parameter (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by t-SNE analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Analysis with Monocle, Monocle2, TSCAN, and StemID did not clearly reconstruct lineage or infer key genes regulating transitions.
source: Analysis of this data with other recent methods such as Monocle and Monocle2 (Trapnell et al., 2014), TSCAN (Ji and Ji, 2016), and StemID (Grün et al., 2016) did not clearly reconstruct lineage or infer key genes regulating transitions (Figure 4A – Bottom, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with other methods shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The iterative clustering procedure converged when the dimension of the re-clustering subspace changed by less than 10% of the total transcription factor space.
source: We iterated the clustering-inference procedure until the dimension of the re-clustering subspace changed by less than 10% of the total transcription factor space.
evidence: The claim describes the convergence criterion for the algorithm.

claim: 45 high probability triplets (p(T | {gi})>0.6) were inferred between the final cell clusters.
source: We inferred 45 high probability triplets (p(T | {gi})>0.6) between the final cell clusters (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the inference analysis.

claim: The c0-c2 transition genes include DMRTA1, HES1, HES5, FOXG1, PAX6, HMGA2, SOX2, SOX3, SOX9, SOX6, SP8, OTX2, TGIF, ID4, SOX3, TCF7L2, and TCFL1.
source: The c0−c2 transition genes include DMRTA1, HES1, HES5, FOXG1, PAX6, HMGA2, SOX2, SOX3, SOX9, SOX6, SP8, OTX2, TGIF, ID4, SOX3, TCF7L2, and TCFL1 which are known to be expressed in forebrain progenitors of the developing neocortex, thalamus, and hypothalamus (Abraham et al., 2013; Pozniak et al., 2010; Shimojo et al., 2011; Tzeng and de Vellis, 1998; Wang et al., 2006), and are known to establish dorsal forebrain regional identity; (Azim et al., 2009; Bani-Yaghoub et al., 2006; Borello et al., 2014; Gaston-Massuet et al., 2016; Hagey et al., 2014; Hutton and Pevny, 2011; Johansson et al., 2013; Kikkawa et al., 2013; Kishi et al., 2012; Manuel et al., 2011; Miyoshi and Fishell, 2012; Ohtsuka et al., 2001; Ross et al., 2003; Shen and Walsh, 2005; Sur and Rubenstein, 2005; Yang et al., 2015; Zembrzycki et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by probabilistic analysis and extensive citations to published work on forebrain development.

claim: The c2-c0 branch is mediated by 39 transition genes including LHX2, FEZF2, FOXG1, HMGA1, SP8, OTX1, SOX11, GLI3, SIX3, and ETV5, suggesting c2 is comprised of cortical progenitors.
source: The c2−c0 branch is mediated by 39 transition genes including LHX2, FEZF2, FOXG1, HMGA1, SP8, OTX1, SOX11, GLI3, SIX3, and ETV5 which suggest that c2 is comprised of cortical progenitors (Appolloni et al., 2008; Greig et al., 2013; Kishi et al., 2012; Manuel et al., 2011; Raciti et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by probabilistic analysis and citations to published work on cortical development.

claim: The c0-c3 branch is mediated by 55 transition genes including GTF2I, HIF1A, ID1, ID3, PROX1, POU3F2, SALL1, SOX21 TCF12, TRPS1 and ZHX2, associated with mesencephalon and metencephalon regional development.
source: The c0−c3 branch is mediated by 55 transition genes including GTF2I, HIF1A, ID1, ID3, PROX1, POU3F2, SALL1, SOX21 TCF12, TRPS1 and ZHX2, which are associated with mesencephalon and metencephalon regional development, as well as having known involvement with midbrain/hindbrain organizer identity (Buck et al., 2001; Enkhmandakh et al., 2009; Inoue et al., 2012; Jaegle et al., 2003; Kunath et al., 2002; Lavado and Oliver, 2007; Milosevic et al., 2007; Ohba et al., 2004; Uittenbogaard and Chiaramello, 2002; Yao et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by probabilistic analysis and citations to published work on midbrain/hindbrain development.

claim: The c2-c4 branch includes transition genes BCL11A, EMX2, FOXP2 and RORB, associated with the neocortex and neuronal identity.
source: The c2−c4 branch includes transition genes BCL11A, EMX2, FOXP2 and RORB, which are known to be associated with the neocortex and neuronal identity (Cánovas et al., 2015; Ebisu et al., 2016; Greig et al., 2016; Jabaudon et al., 2012; Wiegreffe et al., 2015; Woodworth et al., 2016; Zembrzycki et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by probabilistic analysis and citations to published work on neocortex development.

claim: The c3-c5 branch includes transition genes ASCL1, FOXP2, PAX3, POU3F4, ZIC1, ZIC4, HOXB2, and EN2, which regulate fate acquisition in the midbrain/hindbrain.
source: meanwhile is characterized by transition genes in the c3−c5 branch including ASCL1, FOXP2, PAX3, POU3F4, ZIC1, ZIC4, HOXB2, and EN2, which have been shown to regulate fate acquisition in the midbrain/hindbrain (Agoston et al., 2012; Ang, 2006; Di Bonito et al., 2013; Elsen et al., 2008; Hegarty et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2011; Tan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by probabilistic analysis and citations to published work on midbrain/hindbrain development.

claim: The c5-c6 branch includes transition genes PAX3, CRX, SOX11, EBF2, FOXP4, ASCL1, FOXO3, and SIX3, which have strong expression in developing dopaminergic and gabaergic neurons of the midbrain.
source: The c5−c6 branch is inferred from transition genes including PAX3, CRX, SOX11, EBF2, FOXP4, ASCL1, FOXO3, and SIX3 which have strong expression in developing dopaminergic and gabaergic neurons of the midbrain (Agoston et al., 2012; Erickson et al., 2010; Pino et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by probabilistic analysis and citations to published work on midbrain neuron development.

claim: Transition genes in the c5-c7 branch include ARGFX, DUXA, HES1, NFIB, PPARA, SOX2, SOX7, and SOX9, associated with the medulla oblongata region of the hindbrain.
source: Transition genes in the c5−c7 branch include ARGFX, DUXA, HES1, NFIB, PPARA, SOX2, SOX7, and SOX9, which are known to be associated with the medulla oblongata region of the hindbrain (Fawcett and Klymkowsky, 2004; Kameda et al., 2011; Kumbasar et al., 2009; Madissoon et al., 2016; Matsui et al., 2000; Stolt et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by probabilistic analysis and citations to published work on hindbrain development.

claim: Cluster c1 maps to the ganglionic eminences, suggesting an interneuron identity.
source: Specifically, c1, maps to the ganglionic eminences, suggesting an interneuron identity
evidence: The claim is based on correlation with in vivo developmental human data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Clusters c5, c6 and c7 show better mapping to mid- and hindbrain structures.
source: whereas c5, c6 and c7 show better mapping to mid- and hindbrain structures
evidence: The claim is based on correlation with in vivo developmental human data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Cluster c4 appears to be more closely related to neocortex.
source: and c4 appears to be more closely related to neocortex.
evidence: The claim is based on correlation with in vivo developmental human data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The lineage predictions based on the analysis were verified experimentally using viral barcoding in a separate work.
source: These lineage predictions based on our analysis techniques were verified experimentally using viral barcoding in a separate work (Yao et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to experimental validation in Yao et al., 2017.

claim: With as few as 4 genes per triplet, the correct lineage topology could be inferred for all triplets.
source: We found that with as few as 4 genes per triplet, the correct lineage topology could be inferred for all of the triplets.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The dynamics of expression of just four specific genes are sufficient to monitor a particular lineage decision in single cells.
source: Further, these findings suggest that the dynamics of expression of just four specific genes are sufficient to monitor a particular lineage decision in single cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the minimal gene analysis.

claim: Searching for sparse representation of dynamics has the advantage of providing interpretability and experimental direction.
source: Searching for sparse representation of the dynamics has the advantage of providing interpretability and experimental direction (McGibbon and Pande, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McGibbon and Pande, 2017.

claim: Genes showing the clear minimum pattern are most predictive of the sequence of lineage transitions during development.
source: We discovered that genes showing the clear minimum pattern are most predictive of the sequence of lineage transitions during development.
evidence: The claim is based on the pattern discovery analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The clear minimum pattern is consistent with mutual inhibition, which is hypothesized to play an important role in maintaining multi-stable systems and mediating transitions between different stable states.
source: The same pattern observed in many differentiating systems (Graf and Enver, 2009; Qi et al., 2013; Thomson et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 1999), and is consistent with mutual inhibition. Mutual inhibition, in turn, is hypothesized to play an important role in maintaining multi-stable systems and in mediating transitions between different stable states of multi-stable systems (Ferrell, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work on mutual inhibition and multi-stable systems.

claim: Finding small subsets of genes which capture lineage transitions provides a low dimensional subspace that captures the dynamics in genetic networks.
source: Finding small subsets of genes which captures the lineage transitions in cells analogously provides a low dimensional subspace that captures the dynamics in genetic networks and can be useful for modeling (Jang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and citation to Jang et al., 2017.
